"Re Enzo" is an opera in four acts composed by Pietro Raimondi, with a libretto written by Francesco Guidi. Composed in the 19th century, it was first staged on March 12, 1835, at the Teatro Valle in Rome.

The opera is named after and centers around the historical figure of King Enzo of Sardinia, who was one of the illegitimate sons of Emperor Frederick II. Enzo was made King of Sardinia in 1239 and played a prominent role in the Guelph-Ghibelline conflicts in Italy. He was captured by the forces of the Guelphs at the Battle of Fossalta in 1249 and remained a prisoner in Bologna until his death in 1272.

The setting and the premise of the opera build on the dramatic and political tensions of his capture and imprisonment. The opera plots typically provide ample opportunity to explore themes of loyalty, love, intrigue, and power, which are common in operatic narratives of the era.

Due to the relative obscurity of the opera today, specifics about its musical style, major arias, or reception are not very well-documented in widely accessible musical literature. Pietro Raimondi himself is better known for his experiment with poly-operas, blending different operas to be performed simultaneously. "Re Enzo" was one of several operatic works he composed, though none secured a lasting place in the standard repertory.

Opera enthusiasts might find "Re Enzo" intriguing as part of the broader study of lesser-known works and composers of the Romantic era. Its historical context also makes it a point of interest for those studying cultural depictions of medieval European history through the medium of opera.
